summary.text: An alkyne is an unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon–carbon triple bond.
Alkynes with one triple bond and no other functional groups follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, and they are traditionally known as acetylenes.
The triple bond is very strong and much shorter than a double or single bond, and the H–C≡C angle of 180° in acetylene makes alkynes rod-like.

facts.label: Terminal acidity
facts.value: Terminal alkynes have pKₐ values around 25

items.prompt: A model kit shows acetylene as a straight line of four atoms. What feature of the molecule explains that straight shape?

options.label: The hydrogen atoms repel the carbons into a line
The triple bond is longer than a single bond, so it stretches the molecule
Each H–C≡C angle opens all the way out to 180°
The pi bonds bend the carbons around into a small ring

items.explain: The 180° bond angle at the triple bond makes alkynes rod-like.

items.prompt: A chemist tries to build a triple bond inside a ring and finds such molecules rare and hard to keep. What best explains this?

options.label: Bond strain, because the triple bond favours a straight, rod-like shape
The triple bond is too weak to hold the carbons in a ring
Rings can only form from carbon atoms joined by single bonds
The sp orbitals on the carbons all point to the same side

items.explain: Alkynes are rod-like, so cyclic alkynes are rare because of bond strain; benzyne, for example, cannot be isolated.

items.prompt: A chemist wants a hydrocarbon that gives up its hydrogen as H+ most easily. Which kind should she pick?

options.label: An alkene
A terminal alkyne
An alkane
An internal alkyne

items.explain: Terminal alkynes have pKₐ values near 25, far below alkenes (about 40) and alkanes (about 50), and internal alkynes are less acidic than terminal ones.

items.prompt: 3-hexyne has a carbon group attached at both ends of its triple bond. What type of alkyne is it?

options.label: Terminal, because the triple bond sits at the end of the chain
Terminal, because it carries a hydrogen on one triple-bond carbon
Internal, because each triple-bond carbon carries a carbon substituent
Cyclic, because the carbon groups surround the triple bond

items.explain: Internal alkynes have carbon substituents on each acetylenic carbon, and 3-hexyne is a symmetrical example; terminal alkynes have the formula RC≡CH.

items.prompt: Why is the number 3 needed in the name 3-octyne?

options.label: It counts how many triple bonds the molecule contains
It shows the total number of carbons in the chain
It names the group that replaced a hydrogen atom
It shows which carbon the triple bond starts at

items.explain: In parent chains of four or more carbons the name must say where the triple bond is, and the lowest possible number is used.

items.prompt: A chemist compares three carbon–carbon bonds: the single bond in an alkane, the double bond in an alkene and the triple bond in an alkyne. Which is the shortest?

options.label: The single bond in the alkane
The double bond in the alkene
All three have the same length
The triple bond in the alkyne

items.explain: The C≡C distance of 118 pm is much shorter than the C=C distance of 132 pm and the C–C distance of 153 pm.

paragraphs.heading: What an alkyne is
paragraphs.text: An alkyne is an unsaturated hydrocarbon that holds at least one triple bond between two carbon atoms. The simplest ones, with a single triple bond, no ring and no other functional groups, follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. The family's traditional name is acetylenes. That name also belongs to one particular molecule, C₂H₂, formally named ethyne by IUPAC but commonly called acetylene.

paragraphs.heading: A stiff, straight rod
paragraphs.text: In acetylene the H–C≡C angles are 180°. That straight angle gives alkynes a rod-like shape. Forcing such a rod into a ring creates bond strain, so cyclic alkynes are rare. Benzyne, for instance, cannot be isolated.

paragraphs.heading: Short and very strong
paragraphs.text: The triple bond is short. In C₂H₂ it measures 118 picometers, well under the 132 pm of the double bond in C₂H₄ or the 153 pm of the single bond in alkanes. It is also very strong, at 839 kJ/mol. That total breaks down into a sigma bond worth 369 kJ/mol and two pi bonds worth 268 kJ/mol and 202 kJ/mol.

paragraphs.heading: How the three bonds form
paragraphs.text: In valence bond theory, each carbon of the triple bond is sp hybridized: it has two sp hybrid orbitals and two unhybridized p orbitals. One sp orbital from each carbon overlaps with the other's to make one sigma bond. Each p orbital pairs with one on the other carbon, giving two pi bonds and three bonds in all. The second sp orbital on each carbon points the opposite way and can make a sigma bond to another atom, such as a hydrogen in acetylene. Chemists often describe the same bond with molecular orbital theory instead, as overlap of s and p orbitals.

paragraphs.heading: Inside or at the end
paragraphs.text: An alkyne is internal when both carbons of the triple bond carry carbon groups. 3-Hexyne is a symmetrical example, and 2-pentyne a lopsided one. A terminal alkyne, with the formula RC≡CH, has a hydrogen on at least one end of the triple bond. Propyne, also known as methylacetylene, is one, and molecules like it are often made by alkylating monosodium acetylide.

paragraphs.heading: A mildly acidic hydrogen
paragraphs.text: That end hydrogen is mildly acidic. Terminal alkynes, like acetylene, have pKₐ values near 25, against about 40 for alkenes and 50 for alkanes, so they are far more acidic. Removing the hydrogen leaves a carbanion known as an acetylide, and the hydrogen can also be swapped for other groups to give halo-, silyl- and alkoxoalkynes. Internal alkynes are less acidic than terminal ones but still well ahead of alkenes and alkanes.

paragraphs.heading: The alkyne zipper
paragraphs.text: Strong bases can even pull off a hydrogen from the carbon right next to the triple bond, with an estimated pKₐ of 35. Chemists put that to use in the alkyne zipper reaction. It turns an internal alkyne into a terminal one.

paragraphs.heading: Naming alkynes
paragraphs.text: The ending -yne marks a triple bond. In chains of four or more carbons the name has to say where it sits, using the lowest number possible. An octyne whose triple bond starts at the third carbon is 3-octyne, or oct-3-yne. The main chain chosen for the name must include the triple bond, even when a longer chain exists, as long as no higher-ranking functional group is present.
